lessons.title: Firewalls, DMZ and filtering rules
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a brick wall with a guarded door: on the left an Internet cloud, on the right a company network; a green arrow passes through the door, a red arrow is stopped by the wall.
objectives: Tell apart the types of firewall: packet filtering, stateful, application proxy, next-generation and WAF.
Write a filtering policy with default deny and ordered rules.
Place exposed servers in a DMZ.
Know the role of NAT and its limits for security.

references.title: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

blocks.text: What is a firewall for?

A firewall controls the flows between two zones of different trust, for example the Internet and the internal network. It applies a written policy: whatever is not explicitly allowed must be denied. It replaces neither patches nor monitoring: it is one layer of defense in depth.

rows: Addresses, ports, protocol, packet by packet
Does not track connections; broad return rules
The same fields + the state of each connection
The content of the protocol (HTTP, SMTP…)
Applications, users, built-in IPS, TLS inspection
HTTP requests to a web application

blocks.title: Stateful firewall (pare-feu à états)
blocks.text: Firewall that keeps in memory a table of ongoing connections. A response is only accepted if it matches a connection opened from the inside, which avoids opening broad return rules.
Writing the rules

blocks.title: The path of a packet through the rule list
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: the packet arrives, it is compared with the rules from top to bottom, the first matching rule applies, and if none matches the final rule denies everything.

blocks.title: Default deny and rule order
blocks.text: The last rule denies everything (deny all). The most specific rules go at the top: a broad rule placed too early hides the ones below. Each rule has an owner, a justification and a review date.
Firewall: "Whatever is not allowed is forbidden", and the first matching rule wins.

blocks.title: Filtering good practices
items: Filter outbound traffic too: a workstation has no business reaching the Internet on any port.
Deny inbound internal or private source addresses coming from the Internet (anti-spoofing).
Log denials and sensitive rules, and send the logs to the SIEM.
Review the rules at least once a year and remove those no longer used.
Protect firewall administration: dedicated network, strong authentication.

blocks.text: The DMZ

blocks.title: DMZ, demilitarized zone (zone démilitarisée)
blocks.text: Subnet placed between the Internet and the internal network, where the servers that must be reached from outside are installed (web, email, public DNS). If one of them is compromised, the attacker is not yet inside the internal network.

rows: One firewall with three interfaces: Internet, DMZ, internal
An external firewall, the DMZ, then an internal firewall
Two barriers; ideally from two different manufacturers
Hardened exposed server, sole passage point for a service

blocks.title: Forbidden flow: from the DMZ to the inside
blocks.text: A DMZ server must not be able to open a connection to the internal network, except for a precise, justified flow (for example to a database on a given port). Otherwise, compromising the web server becomes a springboard to the whole information system.
NAT: useful, but not a protection

Network address translation (NAT) lets many workstations use a single public address and hides internal addresses. It complicates some attacks, but it is not a security control: only the filtering policy decides what gets through.

Classic trick question: "which firewall protects against SQL injection?". Packet filtering or a stateful firewall does not read HTTP content: a WAF or an application proxy is needed, on top of secure code.

blocks.title: SOC case: a forgotten "temporary" rule
blocks.text: During a review, the analyst finds an "ANY to test-server, all ports" rule, created two years earlier for troubleshooting. The test server no longer gets patches and the logs show regular scans from the Internet. The rule is removed, the server isolated, and the change procedure now requires an expiry date on every temporary rule.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: every rule must have a business owner; otherwise, it is removed at review.
SOC analyst: outbound denials from a server are often the first sign of malware.
Auditor: I ask for the last rule review and look for "any any" rules.
Network administrator: I test every rule change before putting it into production.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: NAT is not a firewall.
Stateful firewall = tracks connections (layer 4); it does not read application content.
The final implicit rule is "deny all", not "allow all".
Servers reachable from the Internet go in the DMZ, never in the internal network.
Types: packet (stateless), stateful, application proxy, NGFW, WAF.
Default deny, specific rules at the top, first match applied.
DMZ: exposed servers isolated from the inside; three-legged or two-firewall architecture.
Filter outbound too, log, review the rules.

lessons.title: Detecting and blocking: IDS, IPS and network access control
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a surveillance camera watching a flow of packets, next to a lifting barrier that stops a red packet.
objectives: Tell apart IDS and IPS, network (NIDS) and host (HIDS).
Compare signature-based detection and anomaly detection.
Interpret false positives and false negatives.

references.title: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS)

blocks.text: Seeing or blocking

rows: Out of band: copy of the traffic (mirror port, TAP)
An attack succeeds while the alert is being read
A false positive blocks legitimate activity
Can cut the network (plan the failure behavior)

blocks.title: IPS, intrusion prevention system (système de prévention d'intrusion)
blocks.text: Device or software placed inline in the traffic, which analyzes flows and blocks those that match an attack.
Network or host

rows: The traffic passing on the segment
The host's logs, files, processes, decrypted traffic
Encrypted content, traffic on other segments

blocks.text: How to detect

blocks.title: Two detection methods
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: signature-based detection is accurate on known attacks but blind to new attacks; anomaly detection spots the unknown but produces more false positives.

blocks.title: False positives and false negatives
blocks.text: A false positive is an alert without a real attack: it wears analysts out. A false negative is an attack without an alert: it is the most dangerous. Tuning an IDS means finding the right balance between the two.
IDS = camera (it watches and warns). IPS = guard at the door (it watches and stops).
Decoys

A honeypot is a fake, isolated system with no legitimate use: any connection to it is suspicious. A network of honeypots is called a honeynet. They are used to detect early and to study attackers' techniques, without ever being connected to real data.
Network access control (NAC) and 802.1X

blocks.title: 802.1X: three actors
blocks.alt: Three-step diagram: the workstation (supplicant) plugs in, the switch or Wi-Fi access point (authenticator) relays the request, the RADIUS server (authentication server) accepts or refuses, then the port opens.

blocks.title: 802.1X
blocks.text: IEEE port-based access control standard: until the device is authenticated (with EAP, against a RADIUS server), the switch port or Wi-Fi access only lets authentication through.
NAC often goes further than 802.1X: it checks the state of the workstation (up-to-date antivirus, patches, encryption) before admitting it, and places non-compliant devices in a quarantine VLAN.

blocks.title: SOC case: the honeypot speaks
blocks.text: A decoy server named like a file server receives, on a Sunday, SMB connection attempts from a workstation in the accounting department. No legitimate user knows this server. The analyst isolates the workstation through the NAC, collects its memory and discovers a network discovery tool launched by malware.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: SOC analyst: a poorly tuned IDS produces thousands of alerts; I want rules suited to our network.
Architect: I place a NIDS behind the external firewall and in front of the sensitive zones.
Auditor: I check that signatures are up to date and that alerts are handled.
CISO: an inline IPS must have a chosen failure mode (fail open or fail closed) according to criticality.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: IDS = passive (alerts); IPS = inline (blocks).
Signatures do not detect an unknown attack (zero-day).
False negative = undetected attack: the most serious case.
802.1X: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server (RADIUS).
IDS out of band (alerts), IPS inline (blocks); network (NIDS) or host (HIDS).
Signatures: accurate but blind to the unknown. Anomalies: spot the unknown, more false positives.
Honeypots: isolated decoys, any connection is suspicious.
802.1X and NAC: authenticate and check the device before opening the network to it.

lessons.title: VPN, segmentation and wireless networks
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a Wi-Fi access point with a padlock, sending waves toward a laptop, and a pipe linking the laptop to the company building.
objectives: Compare site-to-site VPN and remote access VPN, IPsec and TLS.
Explain the risk of split tunneling.
Segment a network with VLANs, subnets and microsegmentation.
Choose the right Wi-Fi security and recognize wireless attacks.

references.title: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs
NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs)
IEEE 802.11i, wireless network security (basis of WPA2)

blocks.text: VPNs

blocks.title: VPN, virtual private network (réseau privé virtuel)
blocks.text: Encrypted and authenticated tunnel across an untrusted network, such as the Internet, that connects a user or a site to the company network.

rows: IPsec in tunnel mode between two gateways
An employee traveling or working remotely
TLS VPN (client or browser) or IPsec with a client
Access to a few web applications

blocks.title: Split tunneling
blocks.text: With split tunneling, only the traffic to the company goes through the VPN; the rest goes straight out to the Internet. It is faster, but the workstation is both connected to the internal network and exposed without the company's protections. A full tunnel sends all traffic through the VPN.

blocks.title: Securing remote access
items: Mandatory multi-factor authentication on the VPN.
Fast patching of the VPN gateway: it is an exposed and heavily targeted device.
Check the state of the workstation before connection (NAC).
Give access only to the applications needed, not to the whole network.

blocks.text: Segmenting the network
A "flat" network, where everyone sees everything, lets an attacker move freely once inside. Segmenting means splitting the network into zones and controlling the flows between them.

rows: Separate logical networks on the same switches (layer 2)
Guest VLAN, server VLAN, telephony VLAN
Separate IP zones, flows filtered by a firewall or ACLs
The guest VLAN only reaches the Internet
Rules at the level of each workload (server, container)
The web server only talks to its database

blocks.title: A VLAN is not a firewall
blocks.text: VLANs separate traffic, but routing between VLANs must be filtered, otherwise the separation protects nothing. Disabling unused ports, not using the native VLAN for users and prohibiting automatic trunk negotiation limit VLAN hopping.
Wireless networks

blocks.title: How Wi-Fi security evolved
blocks.alt: Bars showing the increasing strength of Wi-Fi protocols: WEP very weak, WPA with TKIP weak, WPA2 with AES-CCMP solid, WPA3 with SAE the strongest.

rows: 802.1X with EAP and a RADIUS server, individual credentials for everyone

blocks.title: WPA3 and SAE
blocks.text: WPA3 replaces the WPA2-Personal key exchange based on the passphrase with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline dictionary attacks on a captured handshake.

rows: Unauthorized access point plugged into the internal network
Fake access point imitating the name of a legitimate network
Protected management frames (802.11w), mandatory in WPA3
Searching for Wi-Fi networks while moving around
Unsolicited messages / data theft over Bluetooth
Bluetooth disabled or not discoverable, controlled pairing

blocks.text: Enterprise Wi-Fi: WPA3 (or at least WPA2) in Enterprise mode, 802.1X, verified server certificate, separate guest network.
Hiding the network name (SSID) or filtering MAC addresses are not protections: the SSID shows up in the traffic and a MAC address is easy to copy. In the exam, these are frequent distractors.

blocks.title: SOC case: one access point too many
blocks.text: The wireless detection system reports an unknown access point broadcasting the guest network name, with a very strong signal in the lobby. On an isolated test bench, the team reproduces the scenario and checks that company workstations refuse to connect to it, because they require the RADIUS server's certificate. Security removes the device and a reminder is sent: never enter your credentials on an unexpected Wi-Fi login page.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Architect: I segment by sensitivity and filter every crossing between zones.
SOC analyst: VPN connections from two countries within an hour deserve an alert.
Auditor: I check that WEP and WPA are absent and that the guest network is separated.
CISO: the VPN gateway is a critical exposed asset: patches come first.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Split tunneling = Internet traffic outside the VPN: risk of a bridge between the Internet and the inside.
VLAN = logical separation; routing between VLANs must be filtered.
WEP is broken; WPA (TKIP) is retired; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA3 uses SAE.
Hiding the SSID and filtering MACs do not really protect.
Site-to-site VPN (IPsec tunnel) or remote access (TLS or IPsec); MFA; avoid split tunneling.
Segmentation: VLANs, filtered subnets, microsegmentation, physical isolation.
Wi-Fi: WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise with 802.1X; WEP and WPA to be banned.
Attacks: rogue access point, evil twin, deauthentication, Bluetooth.

flashcards.back: Last rule: deny all. Whatever is not allowed is forbidden.
Read from top to bottom; the first match applies. Specific rules at the top.
Tracks connections (layers 3-4); does not read application content.
Web application firewall (layer 7): SQL injection, XSS.
Next-generation firewall: applications, users, IPS, TLS inspection.
Zone for exposed servers, between the Internet and the internal network.
Translates addresses; it is not a security control.
Limits exfiltration and remote control of malware.
IDS: out of band, alerts. IPS: inline, blocks.
Network: a segment. Host: the machine, including decrypted traffic.
Known and precise / unknown but more false positives.
An isolated decoy: any connection is suspicious.
Supplicant (workstation), authenticator (switch, access point), RADIUS server.
Checks the device's identity and posture; quarantine if noncompliant.
Two offices (IPsec tunnel) / one user (TLS or IPsec).
Internet traffic outside the VPN: the workstation bridges the Internet and the internal network.
Logical separation at layer 2; filter routing between VLANs.
Rules at the level of each server or container.
Broken / withdrawn (TKIP) / AES-CCMP / SAE.
A rogue access point with the same name. Countermeasure: 802.1X with a verified server certificate.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: firewalls, IDS/IPS, VPN, segmentation and wireless
Firewalls: stateless (packets, 3-4), stateful (connections), application proxy (7), NGFW (applications, users, IPS), WAF (web, 7).
Rules: default deny; read from top to bottom; the first match applies; specific rules at the top; an owner and reviews.
Filter outbound traffic too; inbound, refuse internal source addresses coming from the Internet; log denials.
NAT: hides internal addresses, it is not a security control.
DMZ: exposed servers isolated; a three-legged firewall or two firewalls (two vendors); bastion host; no DMZ-to-internal flows except specific ones.
IDS: out of band, alerts. IPS: inline, blocks (risk: a blocking false positive, an outage). NIDS: segment; HIDS: host.
Signatures: precise, blind to zero-days. Anomalies: spot the unknown, more false positives, a learning period is needed.
False positive: alert with no attack (fatigue). False negative: attack with no alert (the most serious). Tune the IDS.
Honeypot / honeynet: isolated decoys, any connection is suspicious.
802.1X: supplicant (workstation), authenticator (switch, access point), authentication server (RADIUS), with EAP. NAC: compliance, quarantine.
VPN: site to site (IPsec tunnel); remote access (TLS or IPsec) with MFA; avoid split tunneling; patch the VPN gateway first.
Segmentation: VLANs (filter routing between VLANs, prevent VLAN hopping), filtered subnets, microsegmentation, physical isolation.
Wi-Fi: WEP broken, WPA (TKIP) withdrawn, WPA2 (AES-CCMP), WPA3 (SAE, protected management frames). Enterprise = 802.1X; Personal = passphrase.
Wireless attacks: rogue access point, evil twin (countermeasure: verified server certificate), deauthentication, wardriving, bluejacking, bluesnarfing.
False friends: hiding the SSID, MAC filtering, NAT: no real protection.

questions.prompt: What should the last rule of a well-configured firewall be?
choices: Deny all
Allow web traffic
Allow all
Log without deciding
questions.explanation: Whatever is not explicitly allowed is denied: the final rule is "deny all".

whyNot.1: Web traffic must be allowed by an explicit rule, higher up.
whyNot.2: Allowing everything defeats the purpose of the firewall.
whyNot.3: A rule must decide; logging is added to the decision.

questions.prompt: Which type of firewall keeps track of open connections so that it only accepts expected replies?
choices: Stateful firewall
Stateless packet filtering
DNS server
Hub
questions.explanation: The stateful firewall keeps a connection table and accepts the replies that match it.

whyNot.1: Without state, each packet is judged on its own, with no memory of connections.
whyNot.2: A DNS server resolves names; it does not filter traffic.
whyNot.3: A hub filters nothing.

questions.prompt: Where should the company's public web server be placed?
choices: In the internal network, near the workstations
In a DMZ
In the administrators' VLAN
Directly on the Internet with no firewall
questions.explanation: Servers reachable from the Internet go in a DMZ, isolated from the internal network.

whyNot.0: Its compromise would open the internal network directly.
whyNot.2: The administrators' VLAN is one of the most sensitive zones.
whyNot.3: Without a firewall, it would be exposed on all its ports.

questions.prompt: Which control can block a SQL injection sent in an allowed HTTPS request to the website?
choices: Packet filtering on port 443
A dedicated VLAN
A web application firewall (WAF)
NAT
questions.explanation: The WAF reads the HTTP content (layer 7) and recognizes injection patterns. The other controls only see addresses and ports.

whyNot.0: It allows or denies port 443 without reading the request.
whyNot.1: A VLAN separates traffic but does not read requests.
whyNot.3: NAT translates addresses; it does not read the content.

questions.prompt: A rule "allow the whole internal network to the Internet" is placed at the top, above a rule "deny workstation X to the Internet". What happens to workstation X?
choices: The firewall reports a conflict and blocks everything
It is blocked, because the most specific rule always wins
It is allowed, because the first matching rule applies
It depends on the time of day
questions.explanation: Rules are read from top to bottom and the first match applies: the broad rule hides the specific one.

whyNot.0: The firewall does not arbitrate: it applies the order.
whyNot.1: Most firewalls apply the first matching rule, not the most specific one.
whyNot.3: There is no notion of time in these rules.

questions.prompt: A colleague says: "We have NAT, so we don't need filtering rules." What is the right answer?
choices: NAT hides addresses but does not replace filtering
NAT replaces the IDS by reporting suspicious connections
They are right, because NAT blocks every attack coming from the Internet
NAT encrypts traffic between the internal network and the Internet
questions.explanation: NAT translates addresses; only the filtering policy decides what gets through, inbound and outbound.

whyNot.1: NAT detects nothing.
whyNot.2: Port forwarding and outbound traffic get through despite NAT.
whyNot.3: NAT encrypts nothing.

questions.prompt: Why also filter outbound traffic?
choices: To limit exfiltration and connections to a C2 server
To speed up Internet access by reducing the number of flows
Because inbound filtering has become useless with TLS
To avoid having to log inbound connections
questions.explanation: A workstation or server only needs a few outbound flows; blocking the rest hinders exfiltration and remote control.

whyNot.1: Filtering does not speed up traffic.
whyNot.2: Inbound filtering remains essential.
whyNot.3: On the contrary, outbound denials must be logged.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a DMZ placed between two firewalls from different vendors?
choices: It makes network address translation (NAT) unnecessary
It removes the need to patch the firewalls
A flaw specific to one vendor is not enough to get through both barriers
It doubles the available bandwidth to the Internet
questions.explanation: Two different firewalls force the attacker to exploit two separate flaws: this is defense in depth applied to the perimeter.

whyNot.0: NAT is an addressing matter, independent of this.
whyNot.1: Patches are still needed on both.
whyNot.3: Adding a device does not increase bandwidth.

questions.prompt: The web server in the DMZ must read an internal database. Which rule is the most appropriate?
choices: Place the database in the DMZ, next to the web server, with no filtering
Allow only the web server to the database, on its port, with logging
Allow the whole internal network to the DMZ and vice versa, all ports
Allow the DMZ to the whole internal network, to avoid blockages
questions.explanation: A precise flow (source, destination, port), justified and logged, limits the use of the web server as a stepping stone.

whyNot.0: Sensitive data would be exposed next to the public servers.
whyNot.2: Broad rules in both directions defeat the DMZ.
whyNot.3: That is exactly the stepping stone to avoid.

questions.prompt: During an audit, which finding about a firewall is the most worrying?
choices: Logging of denied connections
Documented rules, each with an owner
An annual rule review by the CISO
An "any to any" rule created for a test two years ago
questions.explanation: A forgotten permissive rule opens the network wide. The other three findings are good practices.

whyNot.0: That is a good practice.
whyNot.1: That is a good practice.
whyNot.2: That is a good practice.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between an IDS and an IPS?
choices: The IDS detects and alerts; the IPS is inline and can block
The IDS encrypts; the IPS decrypts
The IDS is hardware; the IPS is always software
There is no difference
questions.explanation: The IDS watches a copy of the traffic and alerts; the IPS sits inline and blocks.

whyNot.1: Neither of them is meant to encrypt.
whyNot.2: Both exist in hardware and software form.
whyNot.3: Their position and action differ.

questions.prompt: What is a real attack that triggers no alert called?
choices: A false negative
A true negative
A false positive
A true positive
questions.explanation: False negative: there is an attack, but the tool says "nothing". It is the most dangerous case.

whyNot.1: True negative: no attack and no alert.
whyNot.2: False positive: an alert with no attack.
whyNot.3: True positive: a correctly detected attack.

questions.prompt: What is a honeypot?
choices: A backup server isolated from the production network
An isolated decoy system with no legitimate use
A free VPN offered to visitors
An antivirus installed on exposed servers
questions.explanation: Any connection to a honeypot is suspicious, since nobody has a legitimate reason to connect to it.

whyNot.0: A backup server contains real data.
whyNot.2: A VPN connects networks.
whyNot.3: An antivirus protects a workstation.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of signature-only detection?
choices: It prevents logging
It only works on Wi-Fi
It produces a huge number of false positives
It does not detect an unknown attack (zero-day)
questions.explanation: A signature describes a known attack: a new attack does not have a signature yet.

whyNot.0: It has no link with logging.
whyNot.1: Signatures apply to every type of traffic.
whyNot.2: That is rather the drawback of anomaly detection.

questions.prompt: Traffic to a server is encrypted end to end with TLS. Which tool will best see an attack in the content?
choices: A hub
A NIDS on the network segment
NAT
A HIDS installed on the server
questions.explanation: The HIDS watches the host, where the traffic is decrypted, as well as its logs and processes. The NIDS only sees the encrypted stream.

whyNot.0: A hub detects nothing.
whyNot.1: Without decryption, the NIDS cannot see the content.
whyNot.2: NAT detects nothing.

questions.prompt: In 802.1X, what is the role of the switch or the Wi-Fi access point?
choices: Authenticator, which relays the request to the authentication server
Certificate authority, which signs the certificates
Authentication server, which checks the credentials
Supplicant, which presents its credentials
questions.explanation: The supplicant is the workstation; the authenticator is the switch or access point; the authentication server is usually RADIUS.

whyNot.1: A certificate authority can issue certificates, but it is not an 802.1X role.
whyNot.2: The authentication server is the RADIUS server.
whyNot.3: The supplicant is the workstation.

questions.prompt: Which risk is specific to an IPS compared with an IDS?
choices: A false positive or an outage can block legitimate traffic
It never raises an alert; it blocks silently
It cannot use signatures, only anomalies
It cannot see the traffic, because it only receives a copy
questions.explanation: Sitting inline, the IPS acts on the real traffic: its mistakes and outages have a direct effect.

whyNot.1: It also raises alerts.
whyNot.2: IPSs make wide use of signatures.
whyNot.3: It sees all the traffic since it is inline.

questions.prompt: An IDS produces 5,000 alerts a day, almost all false positives, and the analysts no longer read them. What is the best response?
choices: Disable the IDS until the team has more time
Tune the rules to the environment and prioritize the alerts
Ignore alerts at night and on weekends to reduce the workload
Add a second, identical IDS to confirm each alert
questions.explanation: Tuning reduces the noise without losing detection; alert fatigue creates "human" false negatives.

whyNot.0: All detection would be lost.
whyNot.2: Attacks also happen at night.
whyNot.3: It would double the noise.

questions.prompt: A laptop without recent patches connects to the wired network. What can a NAC solution do?
choices: Nothing, because NAC only looks at the workstation's IP address
Check the device's posture and quarantine it
Disable the workstation's firewall to install the patches
Delete the operating system of the noncompliant workstation
questions.explanation: NAC checks the identity and compliance of the device before opening the network to it, and can quarantine it.

whyNot.0: NAC precisely checks identity and posture.
whyNot.2: That would be the opposite of the goal.
whyNot.3: There is no destructive action of this kind.

questions.prompt: Which statements about anomaly detection are correct? (several answers)
choices: It compares traffic to a baseline of normal behavior
It requires a period of learning normal behavior
It can spot an attack that is still unknown
It never produces false positives
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection learns what is normal, then reports deviations: it spots the unknown, at the cost of false positives.

whyNot.3: It often produces more of them than signatures do.

questions.prompt: Which VPN permanently connects two of the company's offices?
choices: A remote access VPN
A clientless web portal
A site-to-site VPN
A honeypot
questions.explanation: A site-to-site VPN connects two gateways, often with IPsec in tunnel mode.

whyNot.0: Remote access concerns a single user.
whyNot.1: The clientless portal serves a few web applications.
whyNot.3: A honeypot is a decoy.

questions.prompt: Which Wi-Fi protocol is broken and must no longer be used?
choices: WEP
WPA3
WPA2 with AES
questions.explanation: WEP, based on RC4, can be cracked in a few minutes.

whyNot.1: WPA3 is the most recent standard.
whyNot.2: 802.1X is an authentication method, not a broken encryption.
whyNot.3: WPA2 with AES-CCMP is still acceptable.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of segmenting a network?
choices: Removing the need for passwords in each zone
Making Internet access faster for the workstations
Speeding up backups by reducing traffic
Limiting an attacker's movements and the scope of an incident
questions.explanation: An attacker who compromises one zone cannot see everything else: the compromise is contained.

whyNot.0: Segmentation does not replace authentication.
whyNot.1: That is not its purpose.
whyNot.2: That is not its purpose.

questions.prompt: Why is split tunneling a risk?
choices: It encrypts the traffic twice, which weakens the encryption
It prevents the workstation from reaching internal applications
It disables multifactor authentication on the gateway
The workstation connects the internal network to the Internet without protection
questions.explanation: The workstation becomes a possible bridge between the Internet and the internal network.

whyNot.0: It does not encrypt twice.
whyNot.1: Internal applications remain reachable through the tunnel.
whyNot.2: It has no link with MFA.

questions.prompt: Why prefer Enterprise mode (802.1X) over Personal mode for a company's Wi-Fi?
choices: It is easier to install and maintain
Individual credentials: revocation and traceability
It uses no encryption, so it is faster
It avoids having to deploy a RADIUS server
questions.explanation: With a shared passphrase, an employee leaving forces you to change it everywhere; in Enterprise mode, you revoke a single account.

whyNot.0: It is more complex, but more secure.
whyNot.2: It encrypts the traffic.
whyNot.3: On the contrary, it relies on a RADIUS server.

questions.prompt: A rogue access point broadcasts the same network name as the company Wi-Fi. Which measure best prevents workstations from connecting to it?
choices: Filtering the allowed MAC addresses on the access points
802.1X with verification of the authentication server's certificate
Increasing the transmit power of the legitimate access points
Hiding the SSID so that the rogue access point does not know it
questions.explanation: The workstation refuses a server whose certificate is not the expected one: the rogue access point cannot pass itself off as the network.

whyNot.0: A MAC address can be copied.
whyNot.2: The rogue access point can be closer and stronger.
whyNot.3: A hidden SSID is easily discovered in the traffic.

questions.prompt: What does SAE bring to WPA3-Personal?
choices: It disables protected management frames (PMF)
It replaces 802.1X and RADIUS in Enterprise mode
It resists offline dictionary attacks
It removes encryption to speed up the connection
questions.explanation: With SAE, capturing the exchange is no longer enough to test passwords offline.

whyNot.0: On the contrary, WPA3 makes protected management frames mandatory.
whyNot.1: SAE concerns Personal mode.
whyNot.3: WPA3 encrypts the traffic.

questions.prompt: Guest workstations and servers are in two different VLANs, but the router routes freely between them. What can be concluded?
choices: The VLANs should be removed and a single network restored
The separation is ineffective as long as inter-VLAN routing is not filtered
The separation is sufficient, since the VLANs are different
The problem comes from the guest Wi-Fi, not from routing
questions.explanation: A VLAN separates traffic at layer 2; without filtering at the routing level, guests can reach the servers.

whyNot.0: VLANs are useful; they must be complemented by filtering.
whyNot.2: Free routing defeats the separation.
whyNot.3: The problem is routing, not the medium.

questions.prompt: In a virtualized data center, the web server should only be able to talk to its database. Which approach fits best?
choices: Split tunneling on administration connections
Hiding the SSID of the administration network
A single large VLAN for all the data center's servers
Microsegmentation, with rules specific to each workload
questions.explanation: Microsegmentation applies rules as close as possible to each server, even within the same subnet.

whyNot.0: Split tunneling concerns VPNs.
whyNot.1: The SSID concerns Wi-Fi.
whyNot.2: All the servers would see one another.

questions.prompt: Which measures strengthen a remote access VPN? (several answers)
choices: One account shared by all remote workers
Multifactor authentication
Access limited to the applications needed
Fast patching of the VPN gateway
questions.explanation: MFA, patching of the exposed gateway and least privilege greatly reduce the risk.

whyNot.0: A shared account removes traceability and individual revocation.
